event.active_generic_sea_01_baited_distr: They laugh at your bluff and throw their hooks knowing you are alone.
Two fake castaways contradict each other and the ambush collapses before it starts.
Your story does not hold; they close in to verify it.
Their leader hesitates long enough to reveal the hidden boat.
Claim an imaginary escort
You spot the trap just as a hook already bites into your rail.
You spot the second boat hidden behind their sail before it can emerge.
You hesitate one second too long; their skiff presses against your side.
The wounds are painted and a grappling line is hidden under the tarp.
Read their setup
They stop playing injured and show their teeth.
Show them you do not believe it
You keep enough sea between you to force their game into the open.
Give them a wide berth
Two sailors smeared with fake blood wave a white cloth from an intact skiff. Their sail hides something low on the water just behind them.
The Too-Clean Wreck
You turn too late and their bow strikes your side.
You make them cross their own line and force them to let go.
You shake them loose, but the impact tears away a plank.
Your turn leaves their hooks pulling at empty water.
Break their boarding angle
A line tightens around your arm and slams you into the rail.
You throw a hook back into their rigging and jam their attack.
You cut one, but a second still holds the hulls together.
The hooks come free before their crew can haul on them.
Cut the grappling hooks
They grab the money and lose enough time for you to break contact.
Throw them a small purse
The skiff drops its tarp. Three grappling hooks whistle toward your rail as a second boat bursts from behind the sail.
The Hooks Come Out
You chase them just far enough to make clear they are not coming back.
Drive them off
The two boats disappear before a second fight can begin.
Let them run
You send them off with a clear warning instead of a pointless chase.
Give them one warning
Their leader spits out the name of a busy passage before breaking away.
Trade their escape for information
Their boats pull away but stay close enough to shout. Their leader wavers between fleeing, bargaining for an exit, and one last provocation.
Within Shouting Distance
event.active_generic_sea_01_barrel_survi: The barrel rolls under you and you slam hard into the rail.
You lift him with the barrel and lay him flat on deck.
You get him aboard, but he swallows more water before reaching the deck.
You pull him from the water before his hands give out.
Haul him up before he slips
The rescue goes badly and the castaway reaches deck barely breathing.
The medic anticipates every move and has him on his feet almost at once.
The medic stabilizes him, but he is too weak to speak at once.
The medic organizes the rescue and the castaway quickly comes around.
Let the medic direct the rescue
The castaway grabs it. You pull him aboard without taking a special risk.
Throw a line and slow down
A lone sailor clings to an overturned barrel. His former ship is still visible on the horizon, but it never slows and nobody turns back for him.
The Man on the Barrel
You give him a temporary place aboard and he finally settles.
Keep him aboard until a port
You let him recover before deciding anything.
Let him breathe before questions
He admits striking his officer after weeks of unpaid wages.
Demand his story first
The ship refuses to turn back. The silence confirms part of his story.
Signal his old ship
Barely recovered, the sailor says his captain threw him overboard after a pay dispute. The other ship keeps sailing away without answering.
The Abandoned Hand
You simply answer that you have seen them without pretending to understand the message.
They answer with an enthusiastic salute, convinced you know their local code.
You identify an old merchant convention used to ask for news without hailing.
You realize they are mainly asking whether the route behind you is safe.
A distant ship repeats three flags that match no common code. It is clearly waiting for an answer, but does not change heading.
event.active_generic_sea_01_contested_fl: You signal for them to take it and continue without a fight.
Let them have the chest
The hook misses and swings back into your rail.
You lift the chest before their line even hits the water.
Both hooks catch together and jam the chest between the ships.
Your hook catches first and pulls the chest to your side.
Hook the chest first
Your offer sounds weak and the other crew demands everything.
You get a clear agreement and even a witness on each deck.
They refuse the split and throw their hook at the same time as you.
Their captain agrees to split before the lines cross.
Offer a split before hooking it
A salvage chest floats between your ship and another schooner. Both crews nearly throw their hooks at the same moment and freeze.
One Chest, Two Hooks
You leave with more, under curses from the other deck.
Claim the larger share
Your nerve is enough to make them soften part of their claim.
Claim the chest was already yours
The chest holds enough Berrys for both sides to leave satisfied.
Split it evenly
You leave them the money and keep only the satisfaction of avoiding escalation.
Give them the contents
The chest opens on several dry purses. The other captain is already counting coins aloud and watching both your hands.
The Lid Comes Off
event.active_generic_sea_01_crossing_wak: You open so much distance they can no longer force their wake on you.
Break off the crossing entirely
You refuse to be pushed off course. The ships pass far too close.
Hold your line
You raise a sharp signal before their stern has even passed.
Signal their mistake
You take their wake from a distance and avoid contact.
Give way early
A large galleon crosses your heading without slowing and forces you to take its wake broadside. Its crew watches as if yielding were obvious.
The Forced Wake
Their officer bows, admits the fault, and returns to his ship.
Accept their apology
After arguing, the officer pays a small sum to avoid a feud between captains.
Demand compensation
You refuse to waste more time and signal them away.
End it
The officer leaves annoyed, but both crews laugh at the exchange.
Throw their arrogance back at them
Minutes later, a launch leaves the galleon. An officer comes to offer very polite apologies, but only after seeing your reaction.
The Apology Launch
event.active_generic_sea_01_deck_challen: The plank rolls under your foot and you fall hard against your own hull.
You turn at the end of their yard and return to offended silence.
You get back aboard soaked under their laughter.
You cross the plank and return before they finish counting.
Take their plank wager
You throw their challenge back as a joke and both ships move on.
Decline with a laugh
You overplay it and their captain raises the stake against you.
They end up betting against their own champion.
They smell the bluff and keep the upper hand in the negotiation.
You turn their challenge into an almost even wager.
Turn the wager around with words
A loud crew holds speed a few meters away. They push a plank over the water and bet nobody on your ship dares cross it.
The Plank Between Decks
Their captain quietly removes the sailor who had been pinning the plank with his foot.
Call out their cheating
The noise starts again and both decks begin betting on everything.
Accept their second wager
You refuse to prove anything more and resume your heading.
Let them have the last word
You pocket what you are owed and refuse to let the game become a feud.
Take the result and leave
Their captain refuses to let it end simply. He pulls out a second purse and offers to double the wager while his men already start cheating.
One More Wager
event.active_generic_sea_01_distress_lan: They confirm they can talk, but cannot steer their ship.
Answer the signal from a distance
The swell throws the hulls together; your planking takes the hit.
You slide into their dead angle and stop their drift cleanly.
You come in too fast and scrape their hull before stabilizing.
You place your ship within reach without creating a second problem.
Come alongside cleanly
The lanterns shrink behind you.
Keep your course
Even your navigator misreads their drift; the hulls collide.
Your navigator catches them in a pocket of calm water and stops the drift.
The approach stays safe, but costs planking and time.
Your navigator settles both ships side by side.
Let the navigator choose the approach
A merchant brig drifts broadside. Three red lanterns blink from its stern while the crew waves a hawser: its rudder no longer answers.
Three Red Lanterns
You help them brace the rudder long enough to resume their route.
Talk them through a temporary repair
You cut it short before their breakdown becomes your problem.
Leave them to manage
The captain hands over a purse before you pass the hawser.
Negotiate before towing
You take their weight on your line. Their captain promises to remember the gesture.
Take them in tow
Their rudder chain snapped clean through. The captain asks for a tow until they can brace the tiller and continue alone.
The Broken Rudder
event.active_generic_sea_01_drifting_mai: You protect the bag until you can return it without reading a single name.
You spot a coastal courier farther on and return the bag still sealed.
Keep it sealed and signal it
One envelope is enough to identify the mail service that lost the bag.
Read one letter to find an owner
You find a few Berrys tucked into an envelope and keep them.
A tarred mailbag floats intact between two currents. Several envelopes stick out of the closure, but the postal seal still holds.
event.active_generic_sea_01_empty_deck.c: A sheet line snaps under your weight and slams your shoulder.
You immediately see someone left the deck in a hurry, but not overboard.
You board without immediately seeing what is wrong.
You spot fresh tracks and a cabin locked from the outside.
Nobody answers, but three dull knocks come from below their deck.
You refuse to feed your crew to a mystery that asks for nothing.
A loose line gives way during the inspection and damages your own planking.
Your shipwright spots a hatch locked from the deck before you even board.
The vessel looks sound, but the silence remains unexplained.
Your shipwright confirms nobody abandoned this vessel long ago.
Let the shipwright read the vessel
event.active_generic_sea_01_empty_deck.t: A small sailboat keeps almost your speed, sails trimmed and table set, but nobody is visible on deck. A cup still steams beside the tiller.
event.active_generic_sea_01_empty_deck_i: The lock gives and several voices speak at once beneath your feet.
Open the hatch
You step back, but the pounding below deck becomes frantic.
Return to your ship at once
You shift the wrong crate and a tool drops onto your head.
You find the key and fresh prints leading from the deck to a missing boat.
You find nothing more before the knocking starts again.
You find the key hidden beneath a mooring bitt.
Search before opening
Three dull knocks finally answer your calls. The main hatch is locked from the outside, and one key is missing from the ring by the tiller.
Three Knocks Below Deck
Their quartermaster locked everyone below, took the payroll, and fled in the boat.
Question them before leaving
The captain gathers a small sum rather than argue while his ship drifts.
Claim a reward
You let them out and return their ship. Their relief is immediate.
Free the sailors
You simply return the key and let their crew take control again.
Ask for nothing
The hatch opens on a furious captain and several sailors locked below for hours. Their quartermaster vanished with their boat and payroll.
The Locked Crew
Your crew improvises an even more ridiculous flag and the other deck bursts out laughing.
You answer without a real threat, strongly enough that they remember your flag.
Their joke dies on its own without an audience.
Their captain finally lowers the mocking flag without a word.
Stare them down until they lower it
A passing crew raises a crudely painted flag caricaturing your ship. They are clearly waiting to see whether you laugh, get angry, or answer.
event.active_generic_sea_01_fresh_wrecka: You go around the field and leave the pieces behind.
Go around the debris
You follow the wrong line and a timber hits your hull.
You trace the drift almost immediately to an overturned hull.
You circle for too long before finding the trail again.
The debris draws a clear line toward something heavier.
Read the debris drift
You lean too far and hit the rigging while catching your balance.
You spot two people under an overturned hull before they can even shout.
You see nothing until a dull knock sounds from beneath an overturned hull.
A hand briefly appears beneath an overturned hull in the distance.
Search for survivors
Split planks, a boot, and a torn piece of sail pass your hull. The wood is not waterlogged: the wreck happened very recently.
Fresh Wreckage
You guide them from outside until they find the opening themselves.
Keep them talking
The hull drops on you and crushes your hand before being pushed away.
You roll the hull over in one effort and both survivors finally breathe open air.
You lift it enough for one survivor to escape, but the other stays trapped a moment longer.
You make enough room to get both survivors out.
Lift the overturned hull
You use your rigging to gradually free both people.
Rig lines under the hull
Two people breathe in an air pocket beneath a small overturned boat. The hull sinks lower with each wave and the space is shrinking.
Under the Overturned Hull
The heat forces you too close and your rigging catches theirs.
You stop their drift while keeping your sails beyond the flames.
You get close, but a spark burns your planking before you pull away.
You place your ship exactly where the smoke spares you.
You keep your sails intact and shout instructions from your deck.
The rope burns through your grip and you slam onto their deck.
You cross before the flame reaches the yard and clear the way for others.
You make it across, but burn yourself landing near the galley.
You land behind the smoke, close enough to help immediately.
A nearby schooner pours black smoke from its ports. The fire has left the galley and climbs toward the mainmast while the crew panics.
event.active_generic_sea_01_galley_fire_: The chest slips and crushes you against the bulkhead before being shoved away.
You clear both the chest and the burning partition in one effort.
You free it, but the heat burns your arms.
You get the chest overboard before the flames reach it.
You turn their panic into organized movement and limit the injuries.
You sacrifice part of their cargo to smother the main fire.
Someone shouts that their powder store sits behind the already-hot partition. Flames have reached the door, but not the chest yet.
The captain gathers a purse and insists that you take it.
The cook admits leaving an open lamp beside an oil cask.
You leave them their money and depart with their gratitude.
The fire is finally contained. The soot-covered captain looks over the blackened deck, then turns to you with a purse and many questions.
event.active_generic_sea_01_inspection_s: The officer catches the inconsistency immediately and brings his cutter closer.
The officer salutes and nearly apologizes for stopping you.
Your story convinces nobody; they demand to board.
Your story holds well enough to turn the inspection into a verbal check.
Invent passage orders
You reduce speed and their officer moves to routine questions.
Accept the inspection
You cross their bow too closely and tear away a piece of planking.
You position so cleanly that their officer gives up the show of force.
You keep the distance, but with a hard maneuver that strains the ship.
You hold exactly the distance they request.
Hold regulation distance
A government cutter raises the inspection flag and cuts across your heading. Its officer asks identity, origin, and reason for travel without accusing anyone yet.
The Inspection Flag
They find nothing worth stopping the voyage over and return to their boat.
Let them inspect the deck
The officer admits they are looking for a ship of another color and shortens the inspection.
Ask for the exact grounds
A few minutes of tea are enough to lower the tension between both decks.
Turn the inspection into conversation
You accept the questions but not their boots on your deck. They carefully note your flag.
Refuse boarding
The verbal check ends, but the officer now asks to see your deck and hold. He claims to be searching for a reported ship in the area.
The Search Request
event.active_generic_sea_01_medicine_fla: The captain pays before accepting your help.
You wish them luck and keep your distance.
Your medic crosses over with a kit and the fever soon stops climbing.
You show them how to cool the patient and stay until he breathes easier.
A schooner raises the sickness flag and asks for help. Their cook has burned with fever for two days, and nobody aboard knows what to do.
The patient describes the flags and currents seen over the last few days.
He gives enough detail to recognize several silhouettes from far away.
You end the conversation and give them the quiet they need.
The fever drops enough for the cook to speak. He insists on returning the favor before the ships part.
event.active_generic_sea_01_overboard_de: He grabs you at the wrong moment and both of you slam into the hull.
You haul him aboard and open distance before the other ship completes its turn.
You haul him up, but his old ship has already turned toward you.
You get him on deck before the other captain can react.
Pull him aboard before they turn back
Your questions make him panic and he swallows water before answering.
You get his story and the names of two witnesses before even hauling him up.
He shouts too fast to be clear while the other ship turns back.
He explains a wage dispute clearly enough for you to understand the stakes.
Make him explain from the water
You give him something to hold while both captains close in to talk.
Throw him a float without taking him aboard
You hold your heading and leave their dispute behind.
Stay out of it
A sailor suddenly jumps from a nearby cargo ship and swims toward you. His captain turns at once and orders you to send him back without explanation.
The Sailor Who Jumps
Under both crews’ eyes, the captain finally hands over part of the unpaid wages.
Demand his wages be paid in front of you
You refuse to decide for him. The sailor chooses not to return to his old ship.
Let him choose for himself
The other captain pays quickly to get his man back and end the scene.
Return him for payment
You place the sailor under temporary protection. The other captain notes your flag before leaving.
Refuse to send him back
The sailor accuses his captain of withholding months of wages. The other ship immediately offers a purse if you return him without argument.
The Withheld Wages
event.active_generic_sea_01_powder_barre: The first shot sets off two barrels together and the shock hits your hull.
Your gunner sets off the whole line in a chain well ahead of your bow.
The shot clears a path, but throws splinters onto your deck.
Your gunner pops the barrels one by one at a safe distance.
Have the gunner shoot them from range
You clip a barrel that bursts against your hull in a sharp detonation.
You use their drift to pass without ever exposing your broadside.
You get through, but a nearby blast tears splinters from your planking.
You find a safe line through the barrels.
Thread the gap between barrels
You let the line of barrels drift ahead until a gap opens.
Reduce sail and wait
A line of tarred barrels drifts across your route. A short fuse sticks from one and still smokes: someone dumped them recently.
The Tarred Barrels
The captain pays to know exactly where the trapped line lies.
Sell the warning
The captain describes a small raider trying to close off their route for two days.
Ask who is after them
You signal only the immediate danger and resume your heading.
Stay out of the rest
The merchant changes course immediately and thanks you for warning about the charges.
Warn the merchant
A merchant ship appears behind the line of barrels and heads straight toward it. Its captain clearly has not understood what is floating ahead.
The Merchant Behind You
event.active_generic_sea_01_sealed_crate: The hook snaps back and cuts your forearm before the crate bangs into the hull.
You catch it in one motion and set it dry on deck.
The crate bangs your planking before you finally haul it aboard.
You recover it cleanly without losing your heading.
Hook the crate as you pass
The crate disappears in your wake without costing you a minute.
Leave it drifting
You keep it in sight. A cutter soon appears and heads straight for it.
Mark it and wait
A copper-banded crate floats just below the surface, too clean to come from an old wreck. A merchant mark has been scraped off its lid.
The Banded Crate
After a few curses, the captain pays to recover the cargo.
Claim a salvage fee
The captain stares at you for a long moment, then leaves without proof.
Deny seeing it
The lid reveals ordinary navigation instruments. The mystery dies immediately.
Open it before returning it
The cutter takes back its crate and thanks you for avoiding an incident.
Return it without fuss
A cutter slices toward you. Its captain recognizes the crate immediately and demands it back, without explaining why its mark was scraped away.
The Owner Arrives
event.active_generic_sea_01_signal_barte: Your curiosity eventually pulls out details they had not planned to share.
You quickly learn which ports they avoid and which they seek.
The sloop stops signaling and moves off without particular resentment.
Each crew leaves with two or three useful names and one more dubious story.
A sloop matches your heading and raises a string of merchant flags. It offers port and ship news in exchange for your own rumors.
event.active_generic_sea_01_song_across_: Your deck finds the rhythm and both crews trade the same chorus until they part.
Your verse draws laughter, then an even cheekier answer.
Invent a verse to provoke them
The deck becomes percussion and even the quietest crew members join in.
You let their song carry over the water for a few minutes before the wind takes it.
A fishing ship crosses your heading singing loud enough to cover the sails. As you pass, its crew throws the chorus at you like a challenge.
You show them how to raise enough canvas to move under their own power.
You refuse to tie your ship to their problem and continue.
They accept the price and pass over their hawser.
You pass a line and accept losing some speed for them.
A small cargo ship has lost its mainmast and barely moves under a jury sail. Its captain asks for a tow until it can continue alone.
event.active_generic_sea_01_tow_request_: They open a sack: only rope and spare parts, badly redistributed after the break.
They complain, then pay to use your deck as temporary storage.
You tolerate a few sacks as long as they keep the passage clear.
You block the way and the sacks go back to their deck.
Make them take the sacks back
As soon as the towline tightens, their sailors start placing sacks on your deck without asking. Their captain claims he is only balancing his boat.
